newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS-Deutsche surges on strong H1 income gain.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Deutsche surges on strong H1 income gain.

text.p: Deutsche Bank AG on Wednesday sent its share price surging more than five percent by reporting a bigger-than-expected 27.5 percent jump in net income in the first half of 1997.
This year's inexorable rally in financial markets enabled the bank to chalk up strong gains in trading and commission income which offset the negative impact of the weak mark on its costs.

Net income rose to 1.5 billion marks ($823.8 million) from 1.2 billion, beating analysts' forecasts which had averaged 1.36 billion marks. The figures were released in a mandatory statement released ahead of a news conference.
Earnings were driven by trading income which jumped 48.3 percent rise to 2.0 billion marks, and by group net commission income which rose 25.7 percent to 4.1 billion marks.

The news sent Deutsche's shares surging 5.3 percent to an all-time high of 127.50 marks in early bourse trade amid keen investor interest in a sector brimming with merger speculation following Monday's announcement of a megamerger between Bayerische Vereinsbank AG and Bayerische Hypotheken- und Wechsel-Bank AG (Hypo-Bank).

"It's a very good result, the figures were above expectations," said Christine Winkler, banking analyst at Bayerische Hypo-Bank who said she would probalbly raise her earnings forecast for the full year.
Earnings per share rose 26.1 percent to 2.90 marks from 2.30 marks.

Risk provisions fell 35.3 percent to 500 million marks from 800 million marks, reflecting that corporate insolvencies are likely to have peaked. Also, last year's risk provisions were boosted by funds set aside for engineering group KHD AG which Deutsche helped bail out.
Net interest income showed modest growth, rising 7.1 percent to 5.7 billion marks.
But administration costs jumped 26.7 percent to 8.9 billion marks.

Analysts had expected a sharp rise in costs as the weakness of the mark against the British pound and the dollar made it more expensive for Deutsche to maintain and expand its London-based investment banking business.
Winkler at Hypo-Bank said the mark's weakness probably accounted for seven percentage points of the rise in administration costs.
Group taxes rose 20.2 percent to 1.3 billion marks. The group balance sheet total rose 12.4 percent to 996.1 billion marks by June 30 compared with end-1996.
